transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-03-12 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Alex (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Jon (Redwood Perf), Sofia (Redwood Solutions), Mark (Acme ML), Lina (Acme Infra), Nikhil (Acme SRE), Tara (Acme Security)

Summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect): Workshop to align on apples-to-apples benchmark methodology for runtime performance testing across hosted/dedicated/private. Topics: prompt sets, load generation, KV cache behavior, batching profiles, quantization tradeoffs, VPC/on-prem constraints. Action items captured at end.

Transcript:
00:00 Alex: hey everyone, welcome thanks for joining, I think we have about an hour, we'll run through methodology and then open up for specifics.
00:12 Mark: yep, thanks Alex, excited — we've been trying to reproduce some of your public numbers but have noise in our environment.
00:20 Priya: quick intro — I'm Priya, I run performance onboarding, I'll focus on the harness and how we measure p50/p95/p99, and Jon will share some kernel-level stuff.
00:35 Lina: hi all, I'm Lina, I manage the infra side for Acme, mainly on-prem clusters and VPCs. We care about tail latency and predictability.
00:45 Jon: quick note, some terms might come out jumbled, like KV cache sometimes transcribed as K-V cash — apologies in advance.
00:53 Alex: ok first slide — objectives: make the tests reproducible, define prompt sets, unify sequence lengths, and agree on what 'apples-to-apples' means.
01:12 Priya: apples-to-apples for us means same model binary (same quantization), same tokenizer, same warmup, same batching strategy, same request mix. That last one is key — mix of single-turn completes vs multi-turn.
01:33 Mark: question — when you say same model binary, do you mean same quantization bits, or same exact compiled kernel? Our on-prem toolchain compiles different kernels for H100 vs A100.
01:47 Jon: good question. For strict apples-to-apples you want same model weights and quantization, but we accept kernel differences if you log which kernels/triton layers were used. The benchmarking harness will capture kernel mapping.
02:09 Lina: also network influences — VPC NAT, egress firewalls, and SNI termination can add jitter. We need runbooks for isolating network noise.
02:24 Priya: agreed, our runbook includes a dedicated subnet, hosts pinned to NICs, and bursting disabled. We recommend at least 20 minutes of warmup at low qps and then ramp.
02:40 Mark: can you walk through prompt sets — we have internal prompts that are token-heavy, others that are short.
02:50 Priya: we'll share three canonical sets: micro (single-shot short prompts, avg 32 tokens), standard (multi-turn conversation snippets, avg 128 tokens), heavy (long-context completions, avg 1024 tokens). Each set should also have a seq-length distribution file.
03:15 Alex: note — don't mix different temperature/randomness if you're measuring latency; stick to deterministic sampling (greedy/top-k fixed).
03:27 Nikhil: about load generation — do you prefer synthetic clients or replaying real logs?
03:35 Priya: both are useful. For apples-to-apples we usually do two phases: synthetic closed-loop driver to control qps/latency, then open-loop replay of production traces to validate. The harness supports both.
03:50 Mark: closed-loop meaning client waits for response before sending next?
03:54 Priya: yep closed-loop equals concurrency-limited, open-loop is firehose style. We'll define target concurrency and qps.
04:10 Jon: batching behavior — continuous batching vs fixed batch windows matter. In our runtime we do dynamic batching with a max batch size and a latency cap. You should record batch-size distribution per step.
04:30 Lina: how do you capture KV cache hits vs misses? That's important for multi-turn.
04:38 Priya: we instrument per-request metadata: was prefix cached, cache hit fraction, avg cached prefix length. For reproducibility log key-value cache TTL and eviction policy.
04:52 Mark: in our case we saw big p99 improvements once prefix caching engaged. But it's hard to replicate because our conversation session lengths vary.
05:05 Alex: that's why we suggest synthetic sessions with controlled prefix reuse ratios — e.g., 70% cache-hit sessions, 30% cold-start.
05:18 Mark: ok. On quantization — we plan to try 8-bit and 4-bit. Any gotchas?
05:24 Jon: 4-bit quant can change quality/latency in non-obvious ways. Some kernels are slower on certain GPUs for 4-bit ops. Always measure throughput and also run a small eval set to check quality regression.
05:40 Tara: security question — when we run on-prem, how do you get telemetry without sending PII off-prem?
05:48 Alex: we have an opt-in shim: you can send only anonymized metrics and kernel mappings, or run the entire harness locally and share artifacts over S3 inside your VPC. We can also provide a reading-only console instance inside your VPC for dashboards.
06:10 Lina: will there be a standard config file for the harness?
06:15 Priya: yes, we'll send a YAML config with knobs: batch_max_size, latency_cap_ms, concurrency, warmup_seconds, cache_ttl_sec, quant_profile.
06:25 Mark: ramp profile — linear or step?
06:29 Priya: we do both; recommended: 2-minute step ramps plus 10 min steady-state runs for p50/p95, and 30+ minute runs for p99 if you have the time.
06:45 Sofia: another note — record CPU-side queuing and kernel durations; sometimes CPU stalls cause tail latency.
06:55 Nikhil: do you instrument GPU telemetry (SM utilization, memory bw)?
07:00 Jon: yes we collect nvtop/perf counters, PCIe stall metrics, and memory allocator logs. We'll share the list of counters.
07:12 Mark: on the apples-to-apples point, can you provide a mapping for H100 vs A100 equivalent configs? We have only A100 on-prem but Redwood benchmarks often show H100 numbers.
07:24 Alex: we'll produce a normalized baseline: e.g., X tokens/s per model per GPU type, and show how to scale to match throughput targets. But for strict tests use the same hardware family if possible.
07:40 Lina: network policy — our VPC restricts outbound ports, will the harness need to pull containers?
07:47 Priya: we can provide an air-gapped bundle and a small bootstrap image for on-prem install. We'll share checksumed artifacts.
07:58 Mark: let's get into metrics and pass/fail criteria. For us, SLO is p99 < 300ms for standard set, cost target under $Y per 1k tokens — how do you make cost comparable?
08:15 Alex: cost comparability: normalize by tokens generated and include compute amortization, but for on-prem it's about ops cost per token — we'll provide a template. For hosted versus dedicated, measure cost per effective token using same batching and cache assumptions.
08:32 Priya: include cold-start penalties separately. For example, p99_cold_start and p99_steady_state.
08:40 Mark: can you talk about measurement noise and confidence intervals?
08:44 Jon: use multiple runs (n>=5) and report median and 95% bootstrap CI. For p99 it's noisy; prefer extended steady-state runs to reduce variance.
09:00 Nikhil: what about tokenization differences — does byte-pair vs other tokenizers change measured latencies?
09:06 Priya: yes tokenization overhead can be non-trivial for short prompts — include tokenization time in end-to-end latency. We'll provide a tokenizer binary to avoid implementation differences.
09:24 Mark: reference artifacts?
09:26 Alex: we'll attach: harness repo link, standard prompt sets, runbook, and an internal perf sheet. Links: (link: internal/redwood/bench/harness) (link: internal/redwood/bench/prompt-sets)
09:40 Lina: about batching windows — if you set a hard latency cap of 20ms do you drop requests?
09:46 Priya: no we enforce latency cap by flushing batch earlier; it results in smaller batches and lower throughput but keeps tail latency bounded. Log batch flush reasons.
09:58 Mark: measurement detail — should we measure per-token latency or per-response?
10:03 Jon: both. Per-token is useful for long-generation steady throughput. Per-response includes tokenization plus end-to-end.
10:12 Mark: how do you log partial streaming latencies? We stream tokens back to clients; streaming changes perceived latency.
10:20 Priya: record first-token latency and time-to-complete. For streaming benchmarks simulate client buffer ACK patterns to match production.
10:33 Tara: compliance — we need a minimal dataflow diagram showing what telemetry leaves the VPC.
10:40 Alex: we'll draft a diagram and share it; the default config anonymizes IDs.
10:47 Mark: on dataset prompts, can you include adversarial examples to test worst-case memory?
10:53 Priya: yes add some pathological long-token sequences and extremely skewed repetition to stress kv cache.
11:05 Nikhil: question about interrupting requests — preemption and graceful degradation.
11:12 Jon: our runtime supports preemption for higher priority traffic, which can increase tail latency for lower tiers; include priority mixing in the workload to simulate.
11:25 Mark: I'm concerned about quantization inference fallback — some slower kernels appear when quant kernel isn't present.
11:31 Priya: log fallback events and kernel-not-found; the harness will surface fallback rates.
11:40 Lina: what about filesystem IO when loading models on cold start? This has bitten us before.
11:46 Jon: include model load times and overlap with request traffic in cold-start tests; cold-start should be measured end-to-end including model load if your app spawns model loads on demand.
11:59 Priya: runbook item: for cold-starts, ensure the model weights are cached on local NVMe and measure load variance.
12:10 Mark: can we have an example run summary?
12:15 Priya: yes typical summary has table: model_variant, GPU_type, quant_profile, batch_max, avg_tokens_per_request, p50_ms, p95_ms, p99_ms, tokens_per_second, cache_hit_rate. We'll share a template CSV.
12:34 Alex: demo time — Priya will briefly show the harness CLI (brief, not full).
12:40 Priya: (screen) run: ./bench --config configs/acme_standard.yaml --mode closed-loop --qps 50 --concurrency 8 --warmup 600
12:55 Priya: output: csv plus JSON with run metadata; note flags for tokenization-only and streaming emulation.
13:10 Mark: if we run in our environment, what evidence do you need to validate results?
13:15 Alex: at minimum: run JSON, kernel map, nvprof counters, and batch-size distribution. Also a short video/glance at the system during run helps.
13:27 Nikhil: do you require SSO into our console?
13:31 Alex: optional. For on-prem evaluation we usually work with artifacts only; if you want live dashboards we can set up a read-only collector inside your VPC.
13:39 Mark: any gotchas regarding PCIe bandwidth or MPS on A100?
13:44 Jon: yes MPS multiplexing can skew latency; test with and without, and document it. Also check nvlink topology.
13:56 Lina: timeline — we want to start pilot tests next week. Is that realistic?
14:01 Alex: yes if Mark can provide sequence distribution and infra inventory today we can push a harness bundle by 3/14 and run initial pilot runs the week of 3/17.
14:12 Mark: sounds good.
14:16 Priya: final recap of next steps: Alex will share harness + prompt sets; Priya will send YAML templates and baseline H100/A100 mapping; Jon will include perf counter list; Mark will share logs.
14:35 Alex: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar and links.
14:40 (call ends)

Notes on transcript quality: some product/component names may be mis-transcribed; speakers sometimes overlap. The above includes intentional minor transcription artifacts (e.g., "K-V cash", "quantizashun").
